ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Two semicircular circular tubes ab and bc with the same thickness and smooth inner walls are connected together, and are tangent at b, fixed on a horizontal plane. A small ball enters the circular tube from end a with a certain initial velocity, and leaves the circular tube from end c. After the small ball enters circular tube bc from circular tube ab, how does the centripetal acceleration change?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are two connected sections of semicircular circular tubes, marked with three points a, b, and c; the small ball is located near end a, and the direction of velocity is indicated by the arrow v. Circular tube ab is the smaller semicircular tube from a to b, and circular tube bc is the larger semicircular tube from b to c. The two sections of circular tubes are tangent at b, so after the small ball goes from a through ab to b, it enters bc, and the direction of motion is continuous at the connection. Reasoning: The circular tube is fixed on a horizontal plane and its inner wall is smooth; the supporting force of the tube wall only changes the direction of the small ball's motion and does no work. Also because they are tangent at b, the speed of the small ball does not undergo an abrupt change when passing through the connection. The magnitude of centripetal acceleration is a_n = v^2/R. Before entering bc, the corresponding radius in ab is R_ab; after entering bc, the corresponding radius is R_bc. From the figure it can be seen that R_bc > R_ab. When the speed v is unchanged and the radius increases, a_n becomes smaller.
